title: Learning Chance-Constrained MDPs with Bellman Distributional Certificates
claim: Distribution-aware constrained learning reaches chance-feasible near-optimal policies that expectation-based constraints exclude, with a sharp phase transition in sample size.
layout: 4 panels in 2x2 grid: network diagram, then three scatter/line plots with insets
description: A 2x2 grid. Panel (a) is a line schematic of the IEEE 14-bus power network. Buses are black bars numbered 1–14, with a generator at bus 2, an AC source at bus 1, and a green battery icon at bus 14. Panel (b) is a scatter of true return against true violation probability. Blue chance-feasible dots and gray infeasible dots are shown. A shaded blue feasible region is bounded by a vertical dashed line. Blue and orange diamond trails are labeled by sample size N, and an inset zooms in on the cluster. Panel (c) plots optimality gap against samples per state-action pair on a log axis. The blue CCMDP curve drops sharply to zero, while the orange randomized Markov curve plateaus. Gray and orange dashed reference lines are drawn. Panel (d) plots violation probability against expected cost, with green and orange shaded regions, dashed thresholds δ and δd, and an inset. Colors are consistent across panels.
caption: { IEEE 14-bus storage control. (a) DC network with the battery at bus 14. (b) Return--violation landscape of the candidate policy class. Blue and gray dots denote chance-feasible and chance-infeasible policies. Blue and orange diamonds show mean performance of CCMDP and randomized Markov-CMDP, respectively. The indicated \(N\) values denote transition samples per state-action pair. The gray square, light-orange star, and green triangle mark the true-model deterministic Markov reference, mixture Markov reference, and deterministic chance oracle, respectively. (c) Optimality gap \(J^\star_{\mathrm{chance}}-J(\widehat\pi_N)\) versus \(N\). The two curves and shaded bands show the mean and \(\pm1.96\) empirical standard errors from 60 independent empirical-model trials per sample size, conditional on a policy being returned. The gray dashed and light-orange dotted lines show the deterministic and mixture Markov reference gaps, respectively. (d) Violation probability versus expected discounted safety cost. The horizontal and vertical dashed lines mark \(q_P(\pi)=\delta=0.15\) and \(\mathbb E[C_\pi]=\delta d=0.045\), respectively. The green region satisfies the Markov expected-cost condition; the orange region contains chance-feasible policies excluded by that condition. Orange diamonds trace the learned mixtures. The reference markers are as in (b). }
abstract: Safe reinforcement learning (RL) commonly enforces expected-cost constraints, but such expectation-form safety may fail to control the probability of rare high-cost trajectories. Chance-constrained MDPs (CCMDPs) impose a stronger probability-level requirement, but are widely viewed as harder because the chance constraint itself is nonconvex and depends on the full trajectory rather than a Bellman-linear expectation. In this paper, we reveal that this computational difficulty does not necessarily imply a higher statistical price. For tabular discounted CCMDPs with bounded successor support and access to a certified planning oracle, we establish a model-based upper bound, with a matching lower bound up to logarithmic terms. Technically, our key idea is the \emph{Bellman distributional certificate}, which constructs a Bellman recursion for constraint violation probabilities before policy selection. The certificate reduces trajectory-level safety analysis to local transition uncertainty, avoiding a union bound over the potentially exponential number of candidate policies. For stochastic policies, we give a model-free variance-reduced policy-gradient algorithm with a finite-sample expected KKT-residual guarantee and independent validation of every accepted policy. Numerical experiments on synthetic CCMDPs and an IEEE 14-bus energy storage control benchmark illustrate the safety and mechanism behavior of the proposed algorithms.
